interest: This file provides a fascinating lens into the intersection of sports diplomacy, geopolitics, and domestic social paranoia in pre-World War II Japan. It documents how the Japanese government sought the 1940 Tokyo Olympic Games to restore international prestige and legitimacy following its invasion of Manchuria and withdrawal from the League of Nations, sparking sharp debate within the U.S. State Department over whether hosting the Games represented cynical face-saving by an aggressive power or a moderating force against militaristic nationalism. Furthermore, the file reveals how anticipated foreign arrivals triggered an intense 'spy fever' and moral panic among Japanese police, who targeted romantic liaisons between foreigners and Japanese women under the pretext of counter-espionage. Finally, it traces the politicization of Olympic participation through Manchukuo's bid for international athletic recognition and early American public boycott campaigns, culminating in Japan's eventual forfeiture of the Games as its war in China expanded.
overview: This file contains U.S. State Department diplomatic correspondence, memoranda, consular despatches, cross-reference sheets, and press clippings from decimal file 894.4063 (Social Matters: Amusements, Sports, Recreation - Olympic Games) spanning 1936 to 1941, focusing on the awarding, planning, and eventual forfeiture of the 1940 Olympic Games in Tokyo. The records detail diplomatic arrangements and customs courtesies for Japanese Olympic representatives Jigoro Kano and Count Michimasa Soejima, alongside analytical assessments by the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding Japan's political motives for hosting the Games after its international isolation following the Manchurian crisis. The file also chronicles domestic tensions in Japan, including an aggressive counter-espionage and morality campaign by the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Board targeting foreign residents and liaisons with Japanese women ahead of the 1940 Games, controversies over the proposed participation of the puppet state of Manchukuo, growing American domestic demands for an Olympic boycott following escalating Japanese aggression in China, and the ultimate transfer of the 1940 Games to Helsinki.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a State Department memorandum concerning a proposed invitation to a Japanese swimming team to visit Honolulu in 1940.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Schuler), Department of State
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet references a Far Eastern Affairs memorandum addressing a proposal to invite Japanese swimmers to Honolulu in 1940. The Department questioned whether holding such an athletic meet was advisable given the disturbed state of athletics in Japan and negative U.S. public opinion toward Japanese aggressive actions. The proposed competition was ultimately not held.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Meiji University Baseball Team and Japanese Swimmers' Proposed Honolulu Meet

subfiles.about: Diplomatic note from the Japanese Embassy requesting customs courtesies for Olympic invitations commissioner Jigoro Kano arriving at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Ambassador requests that the Secretary of State arrange standard customs courtesies for Mr. Jigoro Kano, Member of the House of Peers and Commissioner of the Committee on Invitations to the Olympic Games in Japan. Kano was scheduled to arrive at the port of Seattle on July 5, 1936, aboard the steamship Heian Maru.
subfiles.title: Note from Japanese Embassy Requesting Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano

subfiles.about: State Department letter requesting the Treasury Department to grant customs courtesies to Jigoro Kano at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State requests the Secretary of the Treasury to authorize Seattle customs officials to extend standard courtesies and free entry privileges to Mr. Jigoro Kano. The request confirms a prior telephone arrangement made on July 2, 1936, concerning Kano's arrival on the Heian Maru.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury regarding Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano
subfiles.to: Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic note informing the Japanese Ambassador that customs courtesies and free entry have been arranged for Jigoro Kano.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State acknowledges the Japanese Ambassador's note of July 2, 1936, regarding the arrival of Mr. Jigoro Kano. The note confirms that the State Department arranged for the extension of customary entry privileges and customs courtesies at the port of Seattle.
subfiles.title: Note from Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador regarding Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano

subfiles.about: Treasury Department letter confirming that customs courtesies were authorized for Jigoro Kano at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: The Assistant Secretary of the Treasury advises the Secretary of State that appropriate customs officers in Seattle, Washington, were instructed to extend customs courtesies and free entry privileges to Mr. Jigoro Kano. The letter confirms action taken in response to Kano's arrival on the steamship Heian Maru on or about July 5, 1936.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department Confirming Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Secretary Hull's memorandum concerning Count Michimasa Soejima and the 1940 Olympic bid.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes a memorandum by Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding Count Michimasa Soejima's mission representing Japan at the Olympic Games. Count Soejima expressed the hope that Japan would successfully secure the 1940 Olympic Games for Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Count Michimasa Soejima and Tokyo's Olympic Bid

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing and critiquing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969 on Japan's Olympic motives.
subfiles.from: Wallace T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This memorandum rigorously reviews Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969, correcting factual inaccuracies regarding treaty abrogation and trade restrictions while criticizing the reporting officer's unobjective tone toward Japan as a 'semi-outcast.' The author emphasizes that Japan's Olympic bid predated the Mukden Incident and was promoted by domestic moderates seeking to broaden international consciousness. It concludes that hosting the 1940 Olympic Games in Japan offers greater potential benefits for international understanding than detriments.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum Critiquing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzing the political and psychological significance of awarding the 1940 Olympics to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the International Olympic Committee's decision to award the 1940 Games to Tokyo, interpreting it as an effort by Japan to overcome diplomatic isolation following its actions in Manchuria and North China. The despatch details widespread domestic jubilation, imperial gratification, and statements by Prime Minister Hirota and Mayor Ushizuka, while highlighting War Minister Terauchi's dissenting view that making a fuss over the Olympics was unbecoming of a great nation. Grew assesses that Japan sought international conferences and goodwill missions to allay foreign suspicions without altering its aggressive policies.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969 on the Significance of Awarding the 1940 Olympic Games to Tokyo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet summarizing a Berlin despatch on German preparations and Hitler's plans for the 1940 Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.from: William E. Dodd, U.S. Ambassador to Germany
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet summarizes Berlin Despatch No. 3014 concerning German athletic planning for the 1940 Tokyo Games. It notes that three German Army officers had already been assigned to train for the modern pentathlon. It also records Adolf Hitler's exuberant declaration that Germany would send a powerful team and transport several thousand German workers to Tokyo as spectators.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding German Army and Government Preparations for the 1940 Tokyo Olympics

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs routing slip noting foreign resident indignation in Tokyo over police campaigns against espionage and foreigners.
subfiles.from: Wallace T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This brief routing note summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 2060 regarding a police campaign in Tokyo to prevent espionage and protect Japanese womanhood from 'immoral foreigners.' Turner notes that foreign residents were indignant over heightened police scrutiny of their private affairs following the February 26 Incident, though he advises colleagues that reading the full despatch is unnecessary.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Routing Memorandum on Tokyo Police Anti-Espionage Campaign
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Eugene F. Dooman, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on an intensified Japanese police campaign targeting foreign men and alleged espionage ahead of the 1940 Olympics.
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Dickover reports on a campaign by the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Board and the Home Ministry to eradicate 'immoral foreigners' and prevent espionage ahead of the 1940 Olympics and the Empire's 2600th anniversary. Police authorities placed hotels and dance venues under surveillance and prohibited Japanese women from seeking autographs from foreign athletes, operating on the dubious premise that waitresses and dancers were passing state secrets to foreign lovers. The despatch warns that this sensationalized official crusade was inflaming xenophobia and risking serious international friction.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 2060 on Relations Between Japanese Women and Foreigners and Alleged Espionage Activities

subfiles.about: Newspaper article reporting on the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Board's plans to surveil foreigners and assign detectives to protect Japanese women.
subfiles.summary: This press report details the Metropolitan Police Board's implementation of a 'positive policy' to safeguard Japanese women from international scandals and espionage before the 1940 Olympics. Detectives were assigned to monitor specific hotels and apartment buildings in Marunouchi, Nihonbashi, and Ochanomizu, with warnings that foreigners maintaining relations with multiple women would face deportation. It also notes planned anti-foreign morality lectures at girls' schools and the deportation of an American Indian jazz band.
subfiles.title: The Japan Advertiser Article: 'Police Will Guard Girls From Aliens'

subfiles.about: Newspaper editorial critiquing the Japanese police campaign against 'immoral foreigners' as irrational xenophobia that damages Japan's international standing.
subfiles.summary: This editorial sharply criticizes the Metropolitan Police Board's anti-foreigner campaign and underlying spy mania, ridiculing the assertion that waitresses and dancers possessed military secrets to pass to foreign paramours. It cautions that sensationalizing such issues in newspapers and school lectures only stirs up anti-foreign prejudice among an otherwise hospitable public. The editorial concludes that generating hostility against foreigners is bad manners and detrimental to national business interests when Japan is trying to attract tourists for the 1940 Olympic Games.
subfiles.title: The Japan Advertiser Editorial: 'Foreigners, Morals and Manners'

subfiles.about: Satirical newspaper editorial mocking police paranoia over foreign spies and romances in pre-Olympic Japan.
subfiles.summary: This satirical editorial lampoons the police panic linking romantic encounters with espionage ahead of the 1940 Olympics, juxtaposing modern paranoia against the classical moral precepts of the Onna Daigaku. It questions why foreigners are held to rigid moral standards while officialdom condones licensed prostitution for Japanese men, tracing the heightened surveillance to post-February 26 incident jitters. The piece ridicules assigning detectives to apartment houses and warns that schoolgirl lectures will merely make Japanese youth view every foreigner with dread.
subfiles.title: The Japan Chronicle Editorial: 'Innocent Maidens and Foreign Spies'

subfiles.about: Published letter to the editor by a Japanese resident strongly defending police measures against immoral foreigners.
subfiles.summary: Writing from Kobe, I. Ueda passionately defends the Metropolitan Police Board's crackdown, asserting that Western foreigners abuse Japanese hospitality, practice free love, and debase Japanese womanhood. He likens modern foreign adventurers to historic colonizers who brought syphilis to the Pacific islands and unfavorably compares contemporary 'Shanghai transhipped adventurers' to honorable foreigners of the Meiji era. Ueda warns foreign critics to conform to Japanese standards and mind their own business.
subfiles.title: Letter to the Editor of The Japan Advertiser by I. Ueda on 'Those Immoral Foreigners'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a Japanese Embassy inquiry regarding legal protections and trademark restrictions for the five-ring Olympic emblem.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records an inquiry by the Japanese Embassy concerning trademark and design registration protections for the five-ring Olympic emblem. In preparing to host the 12th Olympic Games in 1940, Japan requested details on U.S. regulatory controls implemented during the 10th Olympiad in Los Angeles in 1932.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Trademark Protection for the Olympic Emblem

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluating William May Garland's public support for Manchukuo's participation in the 1940 Olympics.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum assesses reports that American IOC member William May Garland endorsed Manchukuo's participation in the 1940 Tokyo Olympics. It reviews Consul Langdon's warnings that Chinese athletes would boycott the Games and that Manchukuo's team would merely be a front for Japanese athletes. The analyst concludes that the Department should not involve itself in Chinese political objections and recommends taking no official action.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Manchukuo's Proposed Olympic Participation

subfiles.about: Covering despatch from the Mukden Consulate transmitting a report on William May Garland's statements regarding Manchukuo and the Olympics.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Mukden
subfiles.summary: Consul William R. Langdon transmits in quintuplicate to the Secretary of State a copy of his Despatch No. 113 to Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping. The enclosed despatch concerns statements made in Mukden by American IOC member William May Garland regarding Manchukuo's participation in the 1940 Olympic Games.
subfiles.title: Mukden Consulate Covering Despatch regarding Manchukuo's Olympic Participation

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on William May Garland's public support for Manchukuo's admission to the 1940 Olympic Games.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Mukden
subfiles.summary: Consul Langdon reports that American IOC member William May Garland publicly supported admitting Manchukuo to the 1940 Olympic Games during receptions hosted by the Manchukuo Athletic Association and the South Manchuria Railway Company in Mukden. Garland predicted approval at the upcoming IOC session in Warsaw with backing from Japanese delegates Jigoro Kano and Count Soejima. Langdon cautioned Garland privately that a Manchukuo team would consist primarily of Japanese athletes and that its inclusion would likely trigger a boycott by China, citing similar Chinese protests at past international gatherings.
subfiles.title: Mukden Despatch No. 113 to Peiping Embassy on William May Garland and Manchukuo's Olympic Bid
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping

subfiles.about: Letter from a New York financier urging the State Department to consider the moral propriety of American participation in the Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.summary: Albert J. Hettinger, Jr., writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull following the resignation of Harvard athletic director W. J. Bingham from the American Olympic Committee over the morality of competing in Japan. Heartbroken by Japanese atrocities in China, Hettinger describes his personal boycott of Japanese goods and financial aid to China. He appeals to Hull to informally evaluate whether American athletes should participate in the Tokyo Olympics given unified American sympathy for China.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. J. Hettinger, Jr., Urging State Department Review of U.S. Olympic Participation in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department letter acknowledging receipt of A. J. Hettinger's appeal concerning American participation in the Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton, writing on behalf of Secretary of State Cordell Hull, acknowledges receipt of Albert J. Hettinger, Jr.'s letter of June 9, 1938. Hamilton assures Hettinger that his views on American participation in the Tokyo Olympic Games have received careful consideration and expresses appreciation for his civic engagement.
subfiles.title: State Department Reply to A. J. Hettinger, Jr., on Olympic Participation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet reporting the transfer of the 1940 Olympic Games to Helsinki following Japan's forfeiture.
subfiles.from: H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, U.S. Minister to Finland
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet summarizes Helsinki Despatch No. 634 regarding the relocation of the 1940 Olympic Games after Japan proved unable to host them. The International Olympic Committee notified Finnish authorities that Helsinki could host the event, and Finnish national and municipal authorities subsequently passed a resolution agreeing to organize the 1940 Games.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Relocation of the 1940 Olympic Games to Helsinki
